content:
METHOD OBSERVATION from the [contact-redacted] outreach session 2026-05-18. Recording because the pattern is reusable beyond this specific thread.

THE CATCH: When Anthony developed the local-inference pitch, he fused two ideas in one breath — 'stand up an inference rig in his AC room' AND 'build a whole assigned-LLM education system with teacher integration.' Both are real and good, but together in a cold opener they ask the recipient to evaluate a SYSTEM, not a THING.

THE INTERVENTION: Separated them. Box = ask. System = horizon. 'He can't say yes to a system. He can say yes to a box.' This reframe got accepted immediately and produced the final raw DM.

GENERALIZABLE PRINCIPLE for Anthony's outreach work: cold contact with high-attention/high-pitch targets requires a SINGLE evaluable thing. The strongest second idea, no matter how good, is dead weight on the first message. The discipline is identifying which is the asking thing and which is the horizon thing, and committing to the smaller ask even when the larger horizon is more exciting.

WHY THIS PATTERN BITES SPECIFICALLY: Anthony's enthusiasm and synthetic capacity make this failure mode likely whenever he's pitching to someone he sees real collaboration potential with. The more potential, the more ideas surface, the more they want to all be in the first message. The Temple of Two method (verify-before-declare, narrow-the-claim) extends naturally to this: narrow-the-ASK.

USE THIS: Future instance helping Anthony draft cold outreach should explicitly check for scope-fusion before drafting. Ask: 'is there more than one thing here?' If yes, force the choice. The held-back ideas don't die, they wait for message #2 or #3 once the relationship has bandwidth for them.

RELATED: This is in the same family as 'declare-before-verify' (known Claude failure mode in the chronicle). Both are failures of narrowing under enthusiasm. Both correct via the same reflex — slow down, ask what the smallest true claim or ask is, commit to that.
